newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel unveils long-awaited privatisation plan.
newsitem.headline: Israel unveils long-awaited privatisation plan.

text.p: The Israeli government unveiled its long-awaited privatisation plan on Wednesday, saying shares in Israel Chemicals, Bezeq Israel Telecom and Zim Israel Navigation were likely to be sold first.

The plan, presented by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief economics adviser, Moshe Leon, and Tsipi Livni, head of the Government Corporations Authority, contained no recommendations about when, how or what percent of any companies would be sold.

The two stressed the government's determination to go ahead with the privatisation process, which has lost momentum in recent years, but they cautioned that market conditions and the need for structural reforms in the industry sectors where government companies operate could delay it.
"I think we are more determined (than governments in the past) to undertake measures and I believe we will do it -- but not over one year rather over several years," Leon said.

Leon said the priority was to sell shares through domestic public offerings, although it would also float shares overseas, sell them by tender, merge and break up companies or sell off assets where appropriate.
"We will give priority to an abbreviated timetable over getting the maximum proceeds," Leon added.

Livni grouped Israel Chemicals, Bezeq and Zim among the companies ready to be privatised this year. The list also included some small property-development companies and a government-owned venture capital fund.
Among the companies she said still required preliminary work before they could be privatised were the state-owned airline El Al and Industrial Development Bank.

The plan does not include the state-owned banks, whose sale is being conducted by the Treasury. Leon said most of the $1.3 billion the government hopes to raise this year from privatisation will come from bank sales.

The plan was reviewed this evening by the ministerial privatisation committee, which includes Netanyahu, Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Justice Minister Tzahi Hanegbi. Leon said the three did not make an operative decisions on the plan.
The first steps towards selling government shares in Israel Chemicals will begin soon, Livni said.
"We hope in the next several days to provide the parlimentary finance committee a mechanism for its privatisation," she said.

The state holds 48.5 percent of Israel Chemicals and Israel Corp a controlling 24.9 percent. The rest of the shares are publicly traded. Livni said the government was already authorised to reduce its holding to 28 percent and would sell shares through a tender.

Regarding Bezeq, Livni said share sales depended on talks with Britain's Cable & Wiress Ltd and said no decision had been taken on how privatisation would proceed. She would not comment on reports that Bezeq's 50 percent-owned Pelephone unit might be privatised first.
Livni said the vouchers plan, which was proposed by the previous Labour government, was not included in the new privatisation plan and that she recommended it not be used.
Under the plan, Israeli citizens would have received vouchers entitling them to buy shares in state-owned companies at a discount to their market price.
